learn.title: Perovskite Solar Cells: Next-Gen Efficiency
learn.intro: Perovskite solar cells are revolutionizing renewable energy with their high efficiency and low-cost manufacturing potential. Unlike traditional silicon-based solar panels, these emerging photovoltaic technologies can be produced using simple solution-processing techniques, making them a promising candidate for widespread adoption in the global energy transition.
learn.c1_text: Perovskites are crystalline materials with a specific lattice structure that efficiently absorbs light and converts it into electricity. Think of them like highly efficient sponges that soak up sunlight and release electrons. These materials can be tuned to capture different parts of the solar spectrum, offering flexibility in design and application.
learn.c2_text: Perovskite solar cells have rapidly improved in efficiency, reaching over 30% in lab settings when combined with silicon in tandem configurations. This surpasses the theoretical limit of single-junction silicon cells (~29%). Their lightweight nature and ability to be semi-transparent open new possibilities for building-integrated photovoltaics.
learn.c3_text: India is investing heavily in next-generation solar technologies through initiatives like the Solar Energy Research Institute of Singapore-India Centre (SERIS-SIC). With a target of 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, perovskite research could play a crucial role in achieving ultra-high efficiency solar installations across the country.

learn.title: Lithium-Ion Battery Storage Explained
learn.intro: Lithium-ion batteries are the backbone of modern energy storage, enabling renewable sources like solar and wind to provide reliable power even when the sun isn't shining or wind isn't blowing. These rechargeable batteries store excess energy generated during peak production periods for use during high-demand times.
learn.c1_text: Imagine a battery like a water tank - when energy is abundant, it fills up (charging); when energy is needed, it releases water (discharging). In lithium-ion batteries, lithium ions move from the cathode to the anode during charging, storing energy in the process. This reversible reaction allows thousands of charge-discharge cycles.
learn.c2_text: Utility-scale battery systems can store hundreds of megawatt-hours of energy. For instance, Tesla's Hornsdale Power Reserve in Australia stores 150 MWh and responds to grid fluctuations in milliseconds. These installations stabilize grids by providing frequency regulation, peak shaving, and backup power during outages.
learn.c3_text: India launched its National Energy Storage Programme to promote battery manufacturing and deployment. The country plans to install 30 GWh of grid-scale storage by 2030. Companies like Exide and Tata Chemicals are setting up lithium-ion manufacturing facilities, supporting India's 500 GW renewable target.

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreements Demystified
learn.intro: Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) are long-term contracts that enable renewable energy projects to secure financing and guarantee electricity sales. They bridge the gap between project developers and buyers, creating stable revenue streams essential for large-scale clean energy investments.
learn.c1_text: A PPA is like a lease agreement for electricity - the developer builds a solar or wind farm and sells the power to a buyer (utility, corporation, or government) at a predetermined rate for 15-25 years. This long-term commitment gives banks confidence to finance projects, reducing risk and lowering capital costs.
learn.c2_text: Companies sign virtual PPAs to meet sustainability goals without taking physical delivery of electricity. Google and Amazon have signed dozens of corporate PPAs globally. These agreements help corporations achieve 100% renewable energy targets while providing developers with creditworthy off-takers needed for project financing.
learn.c3_text: India's renewable energy program relies heavily on tariff-based PPAs signed with distribution companies. As of 2023, over 175 GW of renewable projects operate under long-term PPAs. Recent auctions have seen solar tariffs drop to ₹1.99/kWh ($0.024/kWh), making renewables cheaper than coal in many regions.

learn.title: Solar PV and the Photoelectric Effect
learn.intro: Solar photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using the photoelectric effect - a phenomenon where certain materials emit electrons when exposed to light. This fundamental principle powers everything from rooftop installations to massive solar farms.
learn.c1_text: When sunlight hits a solar cell, photons knock electrons loose from their atoms, creating an electric current. Think of it like wind turning a turbine - except instead of moving parts, solar cells use semiconductor materials (usually silicon) to create electron flow. This direct conversion has no moving parts and operates silently.
learn.c2_text: Solar cells use a p-n junction - two types of silicon doped to create positive (p-type) and negative (n-type) layers. When photons hit this junction, they create electron-hole pairs. An internal electric field separates these charges, generating voltage that drives current through an external circuit when connected to loads like lights or motors.
learn.c3_text: India's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme allocates $2.6 billion to boost domestic solar manufacturing. The country aims to produce 650 GW of solar modules annually by 2026. With 70 GW installed solar capacity by 2023, India ranks 3rd globally in renewable energy attractiveness.

learn.title: Green Ammonia: Clean Fuel Future
learn.intro: Green ammonia represents a breakthrough in clean energy storage and transport, offering a carbon-free alternative to fossil fuels for industries that are hard to electrify. Produced using renewable-powered electrolysis, it can store excess renewable energy and serve as fuel for shipping and agriculture.
learn.c1_text: Green ammonia is made by combining hydrogen (from water electrolysis powered by renewables) with nitrogen from the air. Unlike conventional ammonia which uses natural gas and emits CO2, green ammonia produces zero carbon emissions. Think of it as synthetic fuel made entirely from water, air, and clean electricity.
learn.c2_text: The shipping industry, responsible for 3% of global emissions, is exploring ammonia as a marine fuel. When burned, green ammonia releases only nitrogen and water vapor. However, it requires specialized engines and safety protocols since it's toxic in concentrated form. Pilot projects are underway globally.
learn.c3_text: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MMT annual green ammonia production by 2030. Reliance Industries plans a $70 billion investment in green energy, including ammonia production. With 175 GW renewable targets, India could become a major green ammonia exporter to markets like Japan and Europe.

learn.title: Hydrogen Fuel Cells in Vehicles
learn.intro: Hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity through a clean chemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen, producing only water as a byproduct. This technology powers zero-emission vehicles and offers a promising pathway for decarbonizing transportation sectors that are difficult to electrify directly.
learn.c1_text: A fuel cell works like a battery that never runs out as long as you keep feeding it hydrogen. Hydrogen molecules split into protons and electrons at the anode; electrons flow through a circuit creating electricity while protons pass through a membrane. At the cathode, they recombine with oxygen to form water - no combustion required.
learn.c2_text: Hydrogen vehicles store compressed H2 gas (at 700 bar) in tanks and use fuel cells to generate electricity for electric motors. Refueling takes 3-5 minutes versus hours for battery EVs. Toyota Mirai and Hyundai Nexo are commercial examples, though infrastructure remains limited compared to battery charging networks.
learn.c3_text: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission allocates $2.3 billion to develop hydrogen production and infrastructure. Tata Motors and Mahindra are developing fuel cell buses. Indian Oil plans hydrogen refueling stations in Delhi and Mumbai. The mission targets 5 MMT annual green hydrogen production by 2030.
